extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets and students of poetic craft (readers of Horace/Ars Poetica)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on composing and revising poetry (Horace's Ars Poetica): emphasizes the interplay of Nature and Art, disciplined practice, honest critical revision, and avoidance of flattering or biased audiences. Guidance is oriented to poets seeking craft standards and practical norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and art must both aid the poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Often it is asked whether a praiseworthy poem be due to Nature or to art. For my part, I do not see of what avail is either study, when not enriched by Nature's vein, or native wit, if untrained; so truly does each claim the other's aid, and make with it a friendly league.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good poem requires both innate talent ('Nature') and cultivated technique ('art'). Neither study alone nor raw natural gift suffices; aim to combine them into a 'friendly league.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistent practice, self-discipline, and sacrifice
rubrics_metrics.description: He who in the race-course craves to reach the longed-for goal, has borne much and done much as a boy, has sweated and shivered, has kept aloof from wine and women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attain poetic excellence through long-term training and self-denial: steady practice, hardship, and restraint from distracting pleasures are necessary to reach mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from a master / apprenticeship
rubrics_metrics.description: The flautist who plays at the Pythian games, has first learned his lessons and been in awe of a master.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study under experienced teachers and respect formal instruction; mastery often requires imitation, correction, and guidance from a skilled master.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid boasting and claiming knowledge you lack
rubrics_metrics.description: To-day 'tis enough to say: "I fashion wondrous poems..." 'Tis unseemly for me to be left behind, and to confess that I really do not know what I have never learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not posture or proclaim mastery you haven't earned; false claims and vanity harm credibility. Be modest about limitations and avoid hollow self-praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not seek praise from biased or compromised audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have given or mean to give a present to anyone, do not bring him, in the fulness of his joy, to hear verses you have written. For he will call out 'Fine! good! perfect!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reading new work to people who are predisposed to flatter you (gift recipients, patrons, paid audiences); such audiences produce misleading praise rather than honest evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of flatterers and hired applause
rubrics_metrics.description: Like the crier who gathers a crowd to the auction of his wares, so the poet bids flatterers flock to the call of gain... As hired mourners at a funeral say and do almost more than those who grieve at heart, so the man who mocks is more moved than the true admirer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that flattery (including paid or performative approval) distorts judgement. Do not rely on applause as evidence of quality; seek sincere critical response instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never let a fox's intent (servile motives) ensnare you
rubrics_metrics.description: If you mean to fashion verses, never let the intent that lurks beneath the fox ensnare you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not compose primarily to curry favor, manipulate patrons, or advance personal gain. Artistic integrity requires resisting servile or sycophantic motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit to rigorous correction and delete ill-shaped lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Quintilio si quid recitares, 'corrige, sodes, hoc,' aiebat, 'et hoc.' ... he would bid you blot it out, and return the ill-shaped verses to the anvil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept forceful, specific corrections from a knowledgeable critic; be prepared to erase or rework poorly formed lines rather than defending them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not defend mistakes — revise instead
rubrics_metrics.description: If you preferred defending your mistake to amending it, he would waste not a word more... to prevent your loving yourself and your work alone without a rival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a critic points out real faults, avoid stubborn defenses. Willingness to revise is essential; defensiveness isolates you from useful critique and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: The honest critic's duties (Aristarchus standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: An honest and sensible man will censure useless lines, he will find fault with harsh ones; if they are graceless, he will draw his pen across and smear them with a black stroke; he will cut away pretentious ornament; he will force you to flood the obscure with light, will convict the doubtful phrase, will mark what should be changed, will prove an Aristarchus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper editorial critique should: (a) identify and remove useless or graceless lines; (b) excise pretentious ornament; (c) clarify obscure or doubtful phrasing; (d) mark necessary changes clearly. Seek critics who perform these tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small faults (trifles) matter; attend to details
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Why should I give offence to a friend about trifles?' These trifles will bring that friend into serious trouble, if once he has been laughed down...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor errors or slips can have disproportionate negative consequences (embarrassment, ridicule). Attend carefully to small technical and stylistic points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid becoming a 'crazy' or errant poet; maintain judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: As when the accursed itch plagues a man... so men of sense fear to touch a crazy poet and run away; children tease and pursue him rashly. He, with head upraised, splutters verses and off he strays... then if, like a fowler... he fall into a well, not a soul will care to pull him out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain self-control and reputation. Eccentricity that undermines credibility or reason will lead sensible readers and colleagues to shun you; do not alienate potential allies by irrational behavior or affectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake popular showiness for true poetic worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Ut praeco, ad merces turbam qui cogit emendas, adsentatores iubet ad lucrum ire poeta ... clamabit 'pulchre! bene! recte!' ... reges dicuntur multis urgere culullis et torquere mero, quem perspexisse laborent, an sit amicitia dignus: si carmina condes, numquam te fallent animi sub volpe latentes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public spectacle, flattering crowds, and convivial praise (wine-tested approval) are unreliable indicators. True poetic quality is not proven by staged or intoxicated applause; instead rely on sober critical judgment.
